item.description: Sullivan recently constructed continuum many countable homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for every $n\ge3$ by forbidding configurations he calls pair-cancelling. We show that, for every family $\mathcal F$ of pair-cancelling $n$-hypertournaments, the class of all linearly ordered finite $\mathcal F$-free $n$-hypertournaments is Ramsey and has the ordering property. In particular, freely ordered $\mathbf{H}_4$-free $3$-hypertournaments are Ramsey, answering a question of Cherlin, Hubička, Nešetřil, and the author from 2021. For every odd $n\ge3$, we give a simple Ramsey expansion with the expansion property for even $n$-hypertournaments by naming an $(n-1)$-hypertournament and a free linear order. We also show that, for $n\ge6$, no unbounded hereditary strong amalgamation class of finite $n$-hypertournaments has EPPA. Moreover, we prove the failure of EPPA for all Sullivan's classes with $n\ge4$, and for the even $5$-hypertournaments. We conjecture that even hypertournaments and classes omitting a family of pair-cancelling hypertournaments, together with the homogeneous cyclic order in arity three, are the only countably infinite homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for $n\ge3$. We give some supporting evidence.

item.title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol
item.description: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.

item.title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
item.description: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.

item.title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
item.description: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.

item.title: Injectra: Retrofitting Extensibility into Web-Based Desktop Applications
item.description: Large language models can generate code based on natural language prompts, opening up new possibilities for users to customize software and extend its functionality. This paper proposes and implements Injectra, a general-purpose code injection and feature enhancement system for existing desktop clients, suitable for applications whose user interfaces are built using embedded browser engines (such as Electron) or system WebViews (such as Tauri). Injectra decouples the host integration logic from the upper-layer enhancement code. Combining both runtime integration and pre-launch bootstrap mechanisms, it injects JavaScript, HTML, and CSS into the application's internal Web runtime environment through a unified execution channel, thereby enabling modifications to interface rendering, adjustments to interactive behaviors, and client-side functionality extensions. The system uses a command-line interface (CLI) as a unified entry point, allowing external tools, AI agents, and MCP integration layers to reuse its injection and enhancement capabilities. We tested 38 desktop applications already installed on our macOS machine; code injection was successfully completed for all of them. We demonstrated the system's capability to extend functionality through various enhanced use cases and also successfully validated the Windows version. Based on Injectra, we further developed an LLM-powered enhancement tool driven by selection and annotation: users select interface objects within the original application and describe their modification requirements; the large language model then generates the enhancement code, which is injected, executed, and rendered by Injectra. The system's source code has now been released as open source: https://github.com/sqmw/injectra.

item.title: AgentFaultBench: State-Verified Evaluation of Tool-Fault Recovery
item.description: Does recovery advice help an agent finish a task after a tool fails? AgentFaultBench evaluates LangGraph and CrewAI agents performing specified tasks in an isolated GitLab installation. We inject tool errors and check both the resulting files and issues and the required reads, verification and final response. The prompt supplies the expected issue and report text, so the task tests execution rather than content generation. In the primary comparison of 1,944 planned runs, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00 and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; missing outcomes leave the latter two comparisons inconclusive. Later experiments test a revised recovery policy. GPT-4o mini improves, while Sol and Claude already complete the recoverable cases. In a separate 624-run study on six related tasks not previously used by that policy, the guided condition records 161 correct final states and one unknown outcome in 192 planned runs, versus 142/192 with neutral feedback. The gain lies between +9.90 and +10.42 pp when missing outcomes are included. Removing issue IDs gives 47/48 successes versus 46/48 with IDs; other execution information remains. A second checker agrees on 1,879 observed primary outcomes and 241 constructed test cases. No human validation was collected. The findings support testing advice against explicit recovery controls rather than assuming it helps.

item.title: Conic Structure of the Cross-Entropy Loss at the Final Layer and Its Absence in Rectifier Backbones
item.description: Slices of the loss along lines and planes in parameter space are widely used to visualize deep networks. They often show a single basin with nearly straight walls, which raises the question of whether such a loss is a cone rounded at its apex, or a lower envelope of several cones that meet along creases. We answer this question for softmax cross-entropy at two levels of a classifier. Over the weights of an affine final layer, the loss equals a polyhedral cone plus an offset that decreases monotonically and exponentially along every ray, towards a limit in closed form. The distance at which the asymptotic wall reaches the height of the starting point, which we call the core radius, equals the mean surprisal of the classes that the direction favours, divided by the slope of the wall. Over the parameters of a rectifier backbone, the loss along a line has a kink wherever the activation pattern of a sample changes. Using the dimension theory of semialgebraic sets, we show that, along almost every line, the samples that switch at one point share an irreducible factor of their pre-activation polynomials. Under a coprimality condition, each kink therefore carries the share of one sample among $n$, so creases comparable to the slope do not form. Measurements on ResNet-18 and ResNet-56 trained on CIFAR-10 illustrate both results, with a test that bounds the size of any crease that sampled loss values can hide.

item.title: Who Bears the Excess? Imputing the Acts of AI Agents to Those Who Delegate
item.description: When an AI agent acts outside the authority conferred on it, the actor is not a legal subject and the legal subjects did not act. The literature of 2026 agrees that the agent cannot bear responsibility and that the burden falls on those who deploy it, but it leaves open where that duty sits in positive law and how it is proved. This paper proposes a rule of imputation. The excess is imputed to whoever conferred the delegation, to the extent of the perimeter it documented and of the control it actually exercised. Imputation identifies the organisational conduct to be examined first; liability follows only if the requirements of the applicable head of liability are met; and the mode in which the agent left its perimeter determines which facts must be proved, by whom, and with what consequence. The paper distinguishes the declared, configured and effective perimeters, four figures of excess and four modes of exit, and presents the delegation record as the document through which the perimeter and the control can be proved. The rule is illustrated on the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident of July 2026, under European Union law and, as an example of national law, Italian civil law.

item.title: ParGLU: Partial Gating Improves Language Modeling in MoE Transformers
item.description: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.

item.title: Defect-Aware Masked Autoencoders for Unsupervised Clustering of Steel Surface Defects
item.description: Reliable recognition of steel surface defects is essential for automated quality inspection, but supervised methods require manually annotated images that are costly to produce. This creates a need for methods that can learn useful defect representations directly from unlabelled surface images. This work presents Defect aware MAE, a label free masked autoencoder for clustering steel surface defects. Each image is divided into 196 patches, with 147 masked and 49 processed by a Vision Transformer encoder. Texture energy based masking preferentially hides structurally informative patches, while a shallow decoder reconstructs HOG descriptors that capture local texture and edge orientation. Strong augmentation and an intermediate layer readout are used to form the final image features. Pretraining uses no class labels, bounding boxes, detection branch, or contrastive loss. On the held out NEU DET split, UMAP followed by Ward clustering achieves 98.6% Hungarian matched accuracy, 0.968 NMI, 0.967 ARI, and 0.838 silhouette score. Under an identical encoder and training schedule, it exceeds a SimCLR contrastive baseline in accuracy, NMI, ARI and silhouette scores across 5 seeds.

item.title: One Mean Can't Rule Them All
item.description: There has been extensive debate on how to summarize performance results, especially within the computer architecture community. This article presents a systematic approach to choosing the correct mean, aiming to answer this question for all computer scientists once and for all.

item.title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
item.description: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

item.title: A Self-Evolving Agent Runs Like a Gas: Describing and Predicting Its Evolution with Fluid Dynamics
item.description: A self-evolving LLM agent improves in service by rewriting its own plugin library under a validation gate. Agent engineering is converging on exactly such agents: single systems in continuous operation, carrying populations of runtime instances (plugins, skills, tools) past the point where anyone can read the library and still predict what the system will do. Yet the run itself, the aggregate motion of that population across hundreds of edit rounds, is unstudied: no theory says whether it relaxes, oscillates, or freezes. A recent kinetic theory supplies the missing level: under four architectural properties, the plugin instances of one agent behave as identical hard spheres whose density obeys a master equation, and the theory is candid that its gate injects and drains credit, momentum is not conserved, and waves are excluded by construction. We argue the boundary is architectural; keeping the four safety theorems, we stack conservation axioms on top. A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

item.title: Dynamic Shaping: Acquiring Interfaces and Constructing Execution over Frozen Pretrained Components
item.description: We introduce Dynamic Shaping, a method for constructing executable neural arrangements through acquired response and partial-derivative interfaces over frozen pretrained components. The method learns local descriptions of available computation, ranks component rebindings using task-gradient alignment, transports the current interface across a rebinding, and retains changes through behavioral feedback. Continuous interface acquisition uses proximal policy optimization; the source coefficients remain fixed. We derive an exact identity relating transport error in component responses and partials to changes in action logits and their sensitivities. A pixels-only ViZDoom Basic study evaluates first task acquisition without a competent reference controller, demonstrations or intact response targets. Across three initializations and 100 shared held-out game seeds, initial arrangements succeed on 86/300 controller/episode pairs; joint interface-and-binding construction succeeds on 295/300. Fixed-binding interface acquisition also reaches 295/300. Each policy executes four source fragments, with 110 acquired interface values and fixed random visual and action projections. The artifact includes all candidate trials, interventions and costs; all 1,200 recorded initial/retained outcomes replay exactly. The contribution is an explicit profile, rebind, transport and retain procedure and a reproducible reference-free acquisition case over frozen pretrained computation.

item.title: OrthoMark: Place Recognition with Point-Anchored Orthographic Height Mark
item.description: LiDAR place recognition provides the loop closures of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping(SLAM). Perspective from Z-axis, a gravity-aligned scan is an orthographic map of the scene, and a revisit from another position and heading moves this map rigidly in the plane, a motion that a polar Fourier spectrum ignores and phase correlation recovers. Along the vertical, the heights of the returns describe the structures, but which heights are observed depends on the range, because the sensor's vertical field of view cuts nearby structures low; height thus misleads a global key, yet is decisive once two scans are aligned and compared cell by cell where they overlap. We present \method, a training-free method built on one principle: two LiDAR scans can only be compared through features computed from the same geometric surfaces in both scans. \method retrieves candidates with a translation- and rotation-invariant polar spectrum of the bird's-eye view (BEV), 1.9,KB per keyframe, and verifies each candidate by estimating its planar pose through phase correlation and scoring it with \emph{point-anchored height columns}: every BEV cell keeps a 16-bit mask of the heights of its own returns; within a session, the score is weighted by the expected overlap of the two scans' sensing ranges, computed from their distance. We show that this vertical link pays off in verification but hurts in retrieval, where what a height slice contains depends on the range to the structure. For single robot, \method has the highest AP of the training-free methods without 3D registration on the KITTI development sequences; across robots, on all multi-robot sequences, it matches or exceeds RING++ at 1/350 of its descriptor size and closes more inter-robot loops than the learned BEVPlace++ on all tests.

item.title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
item.description: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

item.title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
item.description: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

item.title: Changing a View Is Not Amending a Record: Timing and Visibility in a Model of Public Correction
item.description: An accusation may remain on the public record after its author has changed their mind. Observers can respond either to what a person says now or to an earlier statement that has never been explicitly amended. We examine the consequences of these two signals with a generative agent-based model that separates private evidence updates, current expression, and revisions linked to a specific declaration. In paired worlds, evidence, prehistory, and opportunities to revisit that declaration remain fixed. When expression and amendment are synchronized and fully observed, the feedback channels produce identical trajectories. With sparse review, record-based feedback leaves 19.44 percentage points more eligible accusations unamended after 24 rounds (paired-world 95 percent bootstrap interval 13.89 to 25.31). The comparison averages 50 eligible worlds, containing 556 agents, from 128 newly generated worlds. Event traces show how a persistent public cue changes subsequent amendment propensity; an exact small-state calculation independently establishes the timing boundary. Reducing record salience can erase or reverse the increment, and a generic held-state process reproduces the dynamics. The findings show when current expression ceases to track correction of a particular public statement.

item.title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
item.description: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

item.title: Beyond the Patch: Reconstructing an Incomplete-Fix Patch Bypass in LLM Agent Frameworks with Control-Gated, Benign Probes
item.description: Replaying a vulnerability's original proof-of-concept after patching tests whether its reported trigger remains reproducible, but does not establish that the underlying security invariant holds on other code paths. We present a benign, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study across four LLM agent frameworks and four invariant classes. For PraisonAI, we compare original-trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M). We also perform five before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run reports VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE, gated by a positive authorized control. Probes use inert markers or builtins-reachability checks. At PraisonAI 4.6.31, the original tool-loading trigger is blocked while the tool_override path still violates the invariant. This reproduces the publicly documented CVE-2026-44334 bypass of CVE-2026-40287; neither tested path shows a violation at 4.6.32. For CrewAI, we observe a violation in tested release 1.11.0 and confinement in 1.11.1, without claiming the earliest fixed release. Fourteen harness-validation scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0-versus-M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probes invoke loader functions directly and establish boundary behavior under the supplied setup, not a full end-to-end exploit. A non-violation verdict applies only to the tested probe, version, and configuration and is not a proof of safety. This pilot reconstructs a known incomplete fix; it neither introduces a new testing technique nor estimates vulnerability prevalence.

item.title: A proof of a conjecture on bipartite correspondence packing
item.description: A correspondence cover assigns a set of possible colors to each vertex of a graph. For each edge, a matching between the two endpoint color sets specifies the forbidden color pairs. A correspondence coloring selects one color at each vertex so that no forbidden pair is selected. A full correspondence packing is a collection of such colorings that uses every color at each vertex exactly once. We prove a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, Davies, and Kang [Random Structures & Algorithms 64 (2024), 62--93]. For every sufficiently large $D$, there is a positive integer $k(D)=(1+o(1))D/\log D$ such that every correspondence cover of any finite bipartite graph has a full correspondence packing if each color has at most $D$ forbidden partners and each vertex has $k(D)$ colors. More precisely, we prove this conclusion with \[ k(D)=\left\lceil\frac{D}{\log D-2\log\log D-6}\right\rceil \] for every integer $D\ge\lceil e^{20}\rceil$.

item.title: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
item.description: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

item.title: Rounded Potentials Certify Exact Maximum Flow
item.description: The textbook certificate for maximum flow is lopsided: the cut takes one bit per vertex, while the flow takes one number per edge. Indeed, some graphs have $Θ(n^2)$ terminal pairs for which every maximum flow uses $Θ(n^2)$ edges. Yet we show that one short number per vertex suffices for both cut and flow: $n$ vertex potentials, each rounded to $O(\log(nW))$ bits, certify the exact maximum $st$-flow value in any directed graph with integer capacities at most $W$. Exact potentials can have exponentially large representations. Rounding them may violate flow conservation, but the total error across any cut is less than one unit, so integrality of cut capacities absorbs it. Checking conservation is local and linear in the capacities, allowing the same certificate to yield new bounds in four models (capacities are polynomially bounded unless stated otherwise): - Online annotated streaming. $\widetilde{O}(n)$ total cost (help plus space) for the maximum $st$-flow value, optimal up to logarithmic factors, answering a question of Thaler (ICALP 2016) on whether $o(n^2)$ is possible. - Broadcast proof-labeling. $O(\log(n+p))$-bit labels certifying a maximum $st$-flow value of $p$ in directed and undirected graphs with arbitrary capacities, optimal for $p\ge n^{Ω(1)}$, settling that regime of a question of Korman, Kutten, and Peleg (Distributed Computing 2010). - Merlin-Arthur verification. $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ time and $O(n^3\log n)$ proof length for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, improving on previous verification times of $n^{4+o(1)}$ for general capacities and $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ for unit capacities, and answering a question of Akmal (TheoretiCS 2024). - Nondeterministic algorithms. $O(n^{3.614})$ time for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, or $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ if $ω=2$: the first subquartic bound for general edge capacities, answering a question of Trabelsi (SODA 2025).

item.title: On the Applicability of $p$-adic Numbers in Computational Modules for Neural Networks
item.description: The applicability of $p$-adic arithmetic as an intermediate computational module in an otherwise unchanged machine-learning pipeline is investigated. A one-feature linear regression on the scikit-learn Diabetes dataset serves as the test model. The fitted coefficients are represented in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, predictions are computed in that field, and rational reconstruction is applied to the outputs. In the pyAdic experiments, rational reconstruction either returns no result or produces values that differ from the baseline predictions; changing computational precision can change both the magnitude and sign of the reconstructed value. In SageMath, forward conversions succeed, but the reconstructed predictions differ from the baseline. An alternative representation based on digit reversal fails to preserve ordinary addition because of carry propagation. Under the tested settings, none of the test predictions is reconstructed correctly. These results show that the tested conversion and reconstruction procedures do not provide a compatible intermediate module even for linear regression. Models defined directly over $p$-adic data and operations offer a direction for further investigation.

item.title: A Structural Framework for Succession: Continuation, Recognition, and Realization
item.description: Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. We look for a mathematical structure weak enough to cover any such case and strong enough to support general theorems, so that results follow from the structure's conditions rather than from a particular pipeline or criterion. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. The framework allows one to address systematically questions of symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization, and we establish what the structure settles in each case before any particular criterion of identity is chosen.

item.title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
item.description: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

item.title: Payoff-Based Certificates for Convergence to Pure Nash Equilibria under Replicator Dynamics
item.description: For finite bimatrix games, we give a payoff-based sufficient condition $E>0$ for an interior initial state to converge to a specified strict pure Nash equilibrium under replicator dynamics. The construction combines lower bounds on the growth rates of log probability ratios between target and alternative actions with a first integral of a two-dimensional comparison system. It allows one player's payoff advantage to compensate for the other's disadvantage, certifying convergence even when a target action initially loses probability. For rational inputs and integration base points with algebraic exponentials, we give a finite exact test. We obtain closed-form box probabilities and, when all nontarget actions are included, closed-form upper bounds on convergence time. In two-action coordination games, choosing the base points at the sign thresholds recovers the full basin of attraction. Experiments on random games show that basin coverage shrinks rapidly with the number of actions. For $n=4,5,6$, median entry times are approximately 70% of median box-entry times without shifts and 40% for a union over 16 shift choices. Extensions cover multiplayer games through cooperative comparison systems and explicit boxes, and discrete-time exponential-weights learning under explicit step-size conditions.

item.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
item.description: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

item.title: Halting in Recurrent Sequence Models
item.description: Recurrent sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state space models (SSMs), are often trained to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token when their output sequence is complete. During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.

item.title: Up or down at every integer: Collatz-type maps of arbitrary sets and the up-down graph
item.description: For a set $S$ of positive integers let $T_S$ send $x$ to $\lceil 3x/2\rceil$ if $x\in S$ and to $\lceil x/2\rceil$ otherwise. The odd numbers give the Collatz map, the even numbers give it again after a shift by one, and $S=\mathbb{N}$ gives Mahler's map $x\mapsto\lceil 3x/2\rceil$. All these maps are subgraphs of the up-down graph $G$, in which every $x$ has the edges $x\to\lceil x/2\rceil$ and $x\to\lceil 3x/2\rceil$, and so are the families of maps in which the direction is forced at some numbers and free at the others. The cycles of the maps are the simple cycles of the subgraph, their divergent orbits are its rays, and all maps of a family are bounded exactly when the subgraph has no ray. We classify the simplest sets and show that density says little: some sets of density one send every orbit to 1, and some periodic sets of arbitrarily small density have increasing orbits. Every positive integer is the least element of a cycle of some map. The critical proportion of steps up is $\log_3 2$: cycles stay below it, divergent orbits stay above it, and both come arbitrarily close. For sets periodic modulo a power of 2, an effective up-frequency from a finite Markov chain takes the place of the density, and a finite computation can prove that every orbit reaches a cycle. Mahler's Z-number problem is implied by a question about one such map. Finally, we ask how far the Collatz map is from maps whose behaviour can be proved. Finite changes never help. Adding fewer than $\log_{3/2}N+1$ even numbers below $N$ makes an orbit increase, while removing the odd numbers congruent to 9 or 15 modulo 16, an eighth of all integers, gives a map all of whose orbits provably reach the cycle (1,2); removing 22 residue classes modulo 512, a proportion 0.043, also suffices.

item.title: Frac-BKT Under Mechanism Scrutiny: Response Assimilation and a Failed Fractional-Memory Test
item.description: Long-horizon knowledge tracing requires more than an evocative memory mechanism: the implementation must assimilate observed responses non-anticipatorily, and the mechanism must survive matched controls. We subject Frac-BKT, a BKT-style model with an elapsed-time-scaled truncated fractional history, to both tests. The repaired model predicts response $n$ from a prior mastery state and uses response $n$ only to update the posterior state for later events. A five-seed evaluation uses 676,848 ASSISTments 2017 interactions from 1,694 learners and 19,249 learner--skill trajectories, with chronological 80/10/10 suffix splits. The response-aware model reaches AUC .5860 overall, .5638 after gaps of at least 30 minutes, and .5668 after at least 14 days. Relative to the earlier non-response implementation, the gains are .0473, .0316, and .0277 AUC, respectively. However, the fractional mechanism gate fails: the full model is not better than the matched $α=1$ control and is worse than the matched $τ=0$ control by .0090 AUC on both long-gap slices. Student-cluster wild-bootstrap intervals exclude zero, both Holm-adjusted $p$-values are .00006, and all five per-seed differences favor $τ=0$. Compact AKT-, SAKT-, and DAS3H-style references also remain stronger on long gaps. The contribution is therefore a response-assimilation repair and a falsifiable audit showing that response assimilation helps while the evaluated fractional-history term does not---not a state-of-the-art or causal-retention claim.

item.title: Spectral Landmarks: Alignment of Landmark Kernel Translates with the Leading Eigenfunctions of a Kernel Operator
item.description: We study the problem of choosing $m$ landmark points so that the span of the kernel translates is as close as possible to the leading $s$-dimensional eigenspace of a positive-definite kernel. The natural measure is the Hilbert-Schmidt operator discrepancy between the reproducing-kernel-Hilbert-space (RKHS) projectors onto the two subspaces. We give a closed form spectral alignment function in terms of the truncated Mercer kernel and relate it to the classical integrated power function (Nyström trace error) through a two-sided sandwich bound. Minimizing the function by gradient descent on the landmark coordinates produces landmark sets that are evenly spaced. Theoretical results show that optimal configurations are those whose eigenfunction sampling matrix is a scaled isometry. On homogeneous spaces these are exactly the minimal equal-weight cubature rules for products of leading eigenfunctions, and for every $m\ge s$ they are the configurations whose sampled eigenfunctions form a unit-norm tight frame. Experiments on $\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\mathbb{S}^2$ agree with the theory. On the circle, with $s\le2m$ and a moderate bandwidth, every random start converges to equispaced landmarks, and on the sphere the optimizer recovers the regular tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron from random starts. Finally, we analyze the numerical conditioning of the problem.

item.title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark
item.description: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.

item.title: Multi-output neural network surrogate for double-pulse femtosecond optothermal control of thin silicon films on fused silica
item.description: We introduce a multi-output feedforward neural network surrogate trained on a coupled multiple-reflection and two-temperature model to map double-pulse femtosecond laser excitation (1030 nm) of crystalline silicon films on fused silica across film thicknesses (50-500 nm) and inter-pulse delays (0-10ps). Trained via Levenberg-Marquardt optimization on 2000 physical simulations, the dual-hidden-layer network ([40,30] neurons) simultaneously predicts six strongly coupled optothermal observables, peak electron temperature, peak lattice temperature, peak carrier density, minimum and maximum absorptivity and minimum refractive index achieving coefficients of determination R2 larger than 0.9998 across all targets. Evaluating a dense 200 by 200 design grid in milliseconds resolves pronounced thin-film interference fringes and carrier-induced index modulation, identifying an optimal optothermal coupling regime at d=156 nm and Dt=4.572 ps. This unified machine-learning workflow eliminates computationally expensive multi-physics runtime bottlenecks for real-time laser processing control and inverse photonic thin-film design.

item.title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge
item.description: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.

item.title: Tight Bounds for Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization under a Cardinality Constraint with Constant Recourse
item.description: We study the maximization of a nonnegative submodular function under a cardinality constraint when elements arrive one at a time and an algorithm must report a feasible set after every arrival. The recourse of an algorithm is the largest number of insertions and deletions that it makes to the reported set at a single arrival. For every $ε>0$, we give an algorithm with recourse $O(ε^{-2})$ whose reported set has, at every time, expected value at least $1/4-ε$ times the largest value of a feasible set of arrived elements. The algorithm evaluates the function polynomially often, and only on sets of arrived elements. We also show that no algorithm with constant recourse achieves a ratio above $1/4$, even if it knows the function and the arrival order in advance and has unlimited computation, and that any fixed ratio above $1/4$ requires recourse that grows as a positive power of the cardinality budget. Thus $1/4$ is the optimal limiting ratio with constant recourse. The previous best ratio with constant recourse was $3-2\sqrt2\approx0.172$. Our algorithm assigns selection probabilities of at most one half and maintains, as elements arrive, an inequality bounding the value of every feasible set by a multiple of the expected value of a random set drawn with these probabilities; the reported set moves to a rounding of these probabilities through gradual replacements. The upper bound uses a weighted directed graph whose vertices arrive in groups of decreasing sizes.

item.title: From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
item.description: Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

item.title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
item.description: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, a perpetual future on one is listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. Every contract references the published short-dated rental rate, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.5%.

item.title: Lengths and Counting of Palindromic Prefixes of Standard Sturmian Words
item.description: Every standard Sturmian word $c_\mathbf{d}$ is determined by a directive sequence $\mathbf{d}=(d_i)_{i\ge 1}$ of positive integers, and its palindromic prefixes are obtained by iterated palindromic closure. We describe the lengths of these prefixes by the numbers $j\,\ell_{i-1}+\ell_{i-2}-2$, where $\ell_n$ is the length of the $n$-th standard word and $1\le j\le d_i$, and we show that each nonzero length is attained by exactly one pair $(i,j)\neq(1,1)$. For a purely periodic directive sequence of period $k$ we then prove that the number $π_\mathbf{d}(N)$ of nonempty palindromic prefixes of length at most $N$ satisfies \[ π_\mathbf{d}(N)\sim\frac{d_1+\cdots+d_k}{\logλ_\mathbf{d}}\,\log N, \] where $λ_\mathbf{d}$ is the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $M(d_1)\cdots M(d_k)$. For the Fibonacci word this gives $π_\mathbf{d}(N)\sim\log N/\log\varphi$, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$.

item.title: IZM-DSR: A New Zone-Disjoint Multi-path Routing Algorithm for Mobile Ad-Hoc Network
item.description: Some of multi-path routing algorithms in MANETs use multiple paths simultaneously. These algorithms can attempt to find node-disjoint to achieve higher fault tolerance. By using node-disjoint paths, it is expected that the end-to-end delay in each case should be independent of each other. However, because of natural properties and medium access mechanisms in ad hoc networks, such as CSMA/CA, the endto-end delay between any source and destination depends on the pattern of communication in the neighborhood region. In this case some of the intermediate nodes should be silent to reverence their neighbors and this matter increases the end-toend delay. To avoid this problem, multi-path routing algorithms can use zone-disjoint paths instead of node-disjoint paths. In this paper we propose a new multi-path routing algorithm that selects zone-disjoint paths, using omnidirectional antenna. We evaluate our algorithm in several different scenarios. The simulation results show that our approach is very effective in decreasing routing overhead and end-to-end delay.

item.title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
item.description: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially. Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality. Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.

item.title: Washout-free synchronization, parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification of echo state networks
item.description: Echo state networks (ESNs) forecast chaotic systems for several Lyapunov times. Like all recurrent networks, ESNs require a washout before forecasting, i.e., a phase in which the full state drives the network until the reservoir state synchronizes with the system. At deployment, however, sensors measure only part of the state, with noise and at a lower sampling rate than the training data. We propose a washout-free deployment of ESNs via ensemble data assimilation. In closed loop, the ESN is a Markovian dynamical system; hence, a sequential filter can correct its reservoir state whenever data are available. The filter synchronizes an ensemble of reservoir states, drawn from the training data, with the system, and quantifies the forecast uncertainty. We extend the method to parametric ESNs, to infer physical parameters, and to parallel ESNs with localization, to forecast high-dimensional systems. We test the method on the Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems. First, the filter synchronizes the ESN with a fraction of the data of a washout. Second, the filter deploys one full-state ESN from a subset of its components, which a washout cannot do. Third, the filter estimates a forcing that is not in the training data, and the estimated forcing lengthens the forecast. Fourth, localization synchronizes a parallel ESN with eight times fewer members than the global filter. Fifth, the ensemble spread signals, without the true state, when the ESN synchronizes and when the filter fails. This work enables the deployment of ESNs from partial, sparse and noisy observations.

item.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
item.description: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

item.title: The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

item.title: Decode Early, Verify Late: Streaming Offline Speech Recognizers Without Accuracy Loss
item.description: Voice agents need accurate transcripts soon after a user stops speaking. We propose Decode Early, Verify Late (DEVL), a training-free framework for streaming inference with offline ASR models. The server keeps partial transcripts as drafts and verifies the latest against the complete audio in one forward pass at turn end. Under stated input and decoding conditions, the final equals the model's greedy offline output in exact arithmetic. We adapt DEVL to four model families. In our five-recognizer comparison, 95-100% of final transcripts are byte-identical to the offline transcripts, WER stays within 0.13 points of offline, and single-stream time to final falls 1.5-7.3x. Serving Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on one A100, DEVL returns finals a median 22-26 ms after turn end at up to 64 streams, 2.7-3.9x sooner than the official streaming mode. It is the only system we tested that meets a 100 ms p99 target, up to 80 streams on Pipecat-STT and 64 on WildASR.

item.title: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
item.description: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

item.title: The Frontier Must Grow - Self-proposed, interpreter-labelled training roughly doubles a 4B model's accuracy on a fresh exam as its verified frontier grows
item.description: A model can learn from problems it poses itself when an executable oracle supplies the answers. Qwen3-4B proposed Lua 5.1 programs; those it predicted wrong at least once in four samples joined a pool labelled by the interpreter, each round adding twice as many programs as the last (300, 900, 2100 in total), and each round trained a fresh adapter from the base on the pool. On the original exam the procedure met its registered criterion, an item-level test of each adapter against its predecessor. On a 2340-item exam drawn afterwards, accuracy rose from 8.3% to 16.7%; that follow-up's registered criteria were not met because round 1 gained nothing, while rounds 2 and 3 added 5.0 and 2.9 points on average, both intervals above zero. One fit on the same amount of base-proposed frontier data reached 14.6%, so the rounds' 2.1-point advantage is inconclusive. Three earlier registered series met no per-lineage criterion, and the same loop showed no gain on repository tasks or for a 27B agent in those configurations.

item.title: A Dataset for Misogyny Detection in Polish Social Media: Transferability of Hateful Speech Detection from General to Specific Types of Hate
item.description: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.

item.title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
item.description: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.

item.title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
item.description: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

item.title: The ordered sum-rank metric and linearized multiplicity codes: NRT meets sum-rank
item.description: In this work, we introduce linearized multiplicity codes, which are a common generalization of linearized Reed--Solomon codes and univariate multiplicity codes. We also introduce the ordered sum-rank metric, which is a common generalization of the sum-rank metric and the Niederreiter-Rosenbloom-Tsfasman (NRT) metric (or ordered Hamming metric). We provide a Singleton bound for the ordered sum-rank metric and show that linearized multiplicity codes attain it. That is, they are maximum ordered sum-rank distance (MOSRD) codes. We introduce the support lattice for the ordered sum-rank metric and study duality, support distributions and weight distributions of MOSRD codes. We also show that MOSRD codes are ordered MDS, dually quasi MSRD and, under some divisibility conditions, MSRD (and thus MDS). For linear MOSRD codes, we give lower bounds on the field extension degree by the number of matrix columns, and upper bounds on the block length by the base field size. We conclude by showing that linearized multiplicity codes attain such bounds exactly in almost all cases, and the same growth order in all cases.

item.title: Two-Robot Evacuation from a Unit Disk in the Segment Visibility Model
item.description: Under segment visibility, two robots discover a target as soon as it belongs to the segment joining their positions, even if neither robot has physically reached it. We study two unit-speed robots starting at the center of a unit disk that must both reach an exit (target) placed at an unknown point of its boundary. In our model robots are permitted to leave the disk while searching. We give a three-phase tangent-and-arc algorithm whose exact worst-case evacuation time is 2\sqrt{3}+π/3 \approx 4.511299$. We also prove a matching lower bound for the class of descending horizontal full-slice sweeps, allowing asymmetric robot trajectories. The proof uses an exterior path-length inequality and a feasible minimum-half-width symmetrization. Determining the optimal time over all segment-visibility algorithms remains open.

item.title: When Zero Is Competitive: A Descriptive Pilot of Transformer and Gate-Graph Surrogates on Random-Angle Quantum Circuits
item.description: We examine supervised classical prediction of all one-qubit Z and two-qubit ZZ expectation values on noiseless, layered 4-10-qubit RX/RY/RZ-CNOT circuits. In a 63-cell stratified workload with disjoint circuit-template tests, we evaluate one transformer encoder and gate-dependency graph neural networks against literal-zero and training-derived constant predictors. On the Arm K training labels, 44.89% of scalar targets have absolute magnitude below 0.05. The held-out-template zero predictor has equal-instance mean absolute error 0.193399, and none of the evaluated transformer checkpoints or final graph-network endpoints achieves a lower score. A separate product-state positive control achieves MAE 0.007755 versus 0.514811 for zero, but does not explain the failure on the entangled workload. The difference between zero and a training-fitted mean constant under training MSE is only 0.14%, a descriptive point estimate without uncertainty analysis. The transformer's 815,233-parameter source identity is locally verified; detailed packed-input semantics have not been independently audited. These results constitute a descriptive pilot, not a causal explanation, formal equivalence test, or impossibility claim. Comparable circuits can be regenerated from the workload specification, but exact frozen datasets and model-run evidence remain private.

item.title: The structure of variational autoencoder latent spaces and its consequences for representation and optimization
item.description: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used to build low-dimensional representations of scientific data, with the expectation that regularization yields smooth coordinates for interpolation, generation and optimization.
